---
title: "An introduction to spatial thinking and analysis using R as a crime mapping tool"
subtitle: "Half-day hands-on workshop"
toc: false
---

This workshop introduces the concepts of spatial data analysis, using crime as our example. The aim is to get acquainted with how we represent place in data, the analytical decisions we make, and how these shape what we can say about crime, policing and criminal justice in the places they occur.

Research on crime and place is very good at telling us **what** happens **where**. It is less good at telling us **why** (Bannister et al., 2019). Keep that in mind today. Every map is built on decisions about representation, and those decisions shape interpretation.

We work through examples in R. All code runs in your browser, so you can edit it and see what changes.

## How it works

- **Run Code** runs a block. Run blocks **top to bottom**.
- **Start Over** resets a block.
- Exercises have `______` blanks, a hint and a solution.
- First load downloads R into your browser (~1 min).

## Pick your route

- **New to R and GIS:** run the code, focus on the questions.
- **Know R:** skip Practical 0. Try the **Know R?** boxes.
- **Know GIS:** see the **From GIS?** boxes for QGIS/ArcGIS equivalents.

## Data

Study area: 8 wards from Manchester city centre to Fallowfield. All open data (OGL v3).

- Crime, June 2019: [data.police.uk](https://data.police.uk/)
- LSOA + ward boundaries: ONS. Contains OS data © Crown copyright.
- Population, Census 2021: [nomis](https://www.nomisweb.co.uk/)
- Licensed premises: Manchester City Council

Adapted from the [Crime Mapping module](https://maczokni.github.io/crime_mapping_textbook/) (Solymosi & Medina, University of Manchester).
